blocks.x: Okay, it's going. I was born of Oscar J. Henry. I was born on June 8th, 1888. The city of New Orleans. Remember just about what part of the city uptown? On Coliseum between Valance and Bordeaux, 4729 Coliseum Street. Pretty far uptown. Did your father play any music? None of my people played music other than my brother and I. We both studied trombone. No, Deanna.
It's running again. I was going to ask a little more about your life, you know, when you played at these bands in Chicago and then when you went on from there, how you got back to New Orleans,

how long it was before you came back and so on. Well, I left here in 19, early part of 19. I was 18, yeah. And I left here, went to Chattanooga. Chattanooga, stayed there a while. I went to Cincinnati. From Cincinnati, I went to Florida, just a floating plaster there. I wasn't playing no instrument. Then I came back to Birmingham and the Dayton flood came through. That was in 19, the latter part of the spring of 18, I believe. And then I went to Dayton and nothing in Dayton. I went over to Chicago. That's where I stayed until May, March till 11, 1930. And I came back in there. The depression was just about to hit us there. The depression. I came in there, thought there'd be something around there. There wasn't nothing there. So I went up to Tuskegee and worked at the trade. The musical business was dead. The musician was about to jump in the river. Yeah, I was bad. There was good. Worked on a hospital up there. And it came back here and it got worse. Then I got on the WPA. I believe I was on everything from the F-E-R, no, from the E-R-A, emergency relief. Oh yeah, I forgot about that. E-R-A. The E-R-A, then the F-E-R-A, then the WPA. And then the WPA, then they come as to separate the teachers from the laborers and the doctors and the lawyers, finding what each fella could do. And so the fella told me that Bob Gilbert was for getting up a stump digger's band. That's what they called it, the stump digger's band. But I was out there in the stumps digging, not digging, but chopping roots and trees and everything else. So I went down to see Bob Gilbert. He was in the Josephine Hutchison's Memorial on Canal Street where the parking lot is now. Where was that they were digging? Was that in the City Park? It was in City Park, but we were way out in the Metri Golf Club. Out that way. The gang I was in was in the back of the Metri Golf Club. I knew they dug some of those lakes and things, I think in City Park during the WPA. They did. Cleaned up all that out there. But I wasn't in that section. So I went to see Bob Gilbert. I showed him my two union cards from Chicago local number 208. He said, you're one of the fellas I'm looking for. You were in 208 up there then, didn't you? So, you're one of the fellas I'm looking for. He said, give me a working card. You don't have to go out there no more. So I never went. And they started the WPA band then with 18 men. That's what I wanted to ask about. You were in that. The first 18 men. The first 18 men. There's Adolph Alexander, a fella named Crump. Frankie Duesen, Wilfred Liddette. I can't name all the fellas that was in there. The rest of them. Remember any other? Joe Mitchell. That's all I can remember.
Do you remember any other trombonists? Dooson you say?
Frankie Dooson and I were the first two trombones in the band.
Was Carnish in there? Do you remember? No, no. Bill Carnish never did get in the band.

Or Sonny Henry? Sonny Henry came in after the band had been organized. Oh, maybe three months. But as the band progressed, they had 167 men in the band. Some could read and some couldn't read. So they said they was going to find out who could read and who couldn't read. So they sent old man Joe Martinez there to break up the band. That's what he was sent there for to break up the band. So when he came, he found so many fellas could read music. He scratched his head. He said, I've got something here I can do something with. So he weeded out all them that couldn't read. And he kept all those that could read. And when he got through Gillingham, them fellas could play anything from William Tell down, with the music or without the music. They could play as much ragtime music without the music as they could play William Tell with the music. So that made a good band. And the first music week that the government put on in the city of New Orleans, we had 57 men that came down Canal Street from Claiborne to Hell and End Station. And we played everything from Stars and Stripes Forever down to Gloria. And when we passed World Lines coming back, we hit Chicago Tribune. And you thought it was thunder when we hit Chicago Tribune.
They had a good band.

But somehow they didn't keep the band up. They come and people get and work. And the band went down to three or four men. And I got disgusted and I left the band. And the fellow offered me more and more there to trade. And I just went on back to trade.
Did Martinez stand up and conduct the band with the guitar? Or how did he do it?

Well, Martinez was more of a supervisor of the band. Louis DeMaine was the director. He actually directed the band. He actually directed the band. But Martinez supervised the playing of the music. If the parts didn't sound right, he'd come down and look them over and tell you what note he wanted playing. Because he was a professional piano player himself.
Did Louis DeMaine ever play his trumpet?
He played trumpet. We had George McCullum, George Feuerbos, Big Hater Eddie Johnson with Little World Lines. Little, that little fella play saxophone. Oh shit. Was Handy in that?
No, Handy wasn't in there. Handy wasn't in there.

In the Reed section they had Wiesel Garman, Willie Umphrey, Joe Mitchell, the clarinets, and a fella by the name of the downtown. Can't think of that fella's name. From the clarinet? Oh, clarinet. Wasn't Joe Thomas, was it when they called him? No, no it wasn't Joe Thomas. I can't remember any real tall, Burbank. No this boy live down on�����������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������������
Still around.
Yeah, he's still around. He's still living.
In clarinet.

They had little Eddie Johnson on sax. They had Sidney Cades on banjo. Montague on drums. Sae Frazier on drums. Oily Strapani played bass drum. Old man Joe Howard played bass. Little William Brown played bass. They had Sonny Henry. Harrison Barnes over the river. Lewis Nelson and myself on trombone. They had George McCollum. Line up for a bass. Lewis DeMaine. Gilbert Young. And Bob used to play down at Valentis on trumpet. He played bass down there, Steve Valentis.
Oh, Rico.
Rico. Rico. He was on trumpet.
Well, I think of it. Your nickname, they call you Chickens. Yeah, Chick. How did you get that name, if you don't mind telling us?

No, I don't mind telling us. You see, when we was out in the field, on the WPA, I knew more about chickens than any other fellow out there. In fact, at one time, I could tell you, name every part of a chicken from the top of his comb down to the bottom of his feet. And from his build to his tail. So, one fellow said, look at Chick. Oh, no, they said, look at Chicken Man. They called me Chicken Man. And so, from that one on to the other, what did they say, Chicken Man? So, when they come in the musicians' union here, they called me Chick. So, the nickname just stayed Chick. Now, there's more fellows know me by Chick. You say, you know the trombone player they call Chick? Sure. Now, you ask them, you know Oscar Henry? No.
What about the J in your name?
It's Joseph.
I knew that, but I wanted to use it. Yeah, we didn't know that.

J is for Joseph. My name is Oscar Joseph Henry. Any of your children play music? No, none of them play music. I offered to know him one fellow. If this fellow was around me, I'd like him how to read music. He lives in Minneapolis, Minnesota. Oh, hell.
Oh, hell.
He's just down here on a trip.
If you want to answer the phone, it's all right. We can stop this at any time. It's all right.
Take a nice in the back.
That's your wife. She's catching the back. I'm going to ask about the dance band work. If you ever played many dances or in any dance orchestra or just mostly brass bands.

I play anything, dance, jobs, sit down in the pit, any place where they're playing. Because when I learned how to play, I learned how to play everything just to be played, wherever the man wants you to play. Second, third, fourth trombone, anything on the trombone.

Well, you were telling about that system once, developing your lips the way you practiced with the... Well, I get much of the scouting. Oh, sure. All right. I'll stop it. Well, you have just your slide there.
Just use the slide. You see? You put your thumb in.
On the end of the slide.
See how I pulled your lips?

Yeah. And you just work the slide up and down as if you're playing. But you keep that sort of like pumping, sucking pressure there on your lip. Take the bell off and put your thumb over there and make a vacuum ring. And you figure that strengthens... It does. It pulls the muscles in your lips. Pulls the muscles there.

It makes them super. Because my partner, he said that was our monk. But I have a warner. You see, the man that showed me was a professional trombone player. Sometimes your lips don't vibrate properly.
Sure.
And if you wake them, get them super in the morning...
You work on that a little bit each?
Just before you get ready to go play.
Just before you play. You still like to warm up.
You warm your lips up. See, you get your muscles pulled up. And then after you get your muscles pulled up, well then you don't have no trouble. Your lips vibrate properly. You put that in yourself.
I put that in myself. Using a great big cart there so it can't leak around.
It don't leak. See how that fits in there?
Oh yeah. That's a nice job. I'm not going to have to do that with my cornet.
I just take some of that paste glue and put it on here and stick it in there.
And press it down.
Press it down. Now when this wears out from the water, I just take and cut another cork. Yeah. Just like you get one of these corks out of a whiskey bottle.
Yeah, about three quarters or two thirds of an inch.
Well, you can use any pint cork or half pint cork and you cut it to suit the valve, you know. Yeah.
What make is that trombone you have there?
It's a Harry B.J.

Oh, let me look at it. Can I see the bell? I've never, you know, never seen one of those horns close by. Several people told me they used those horns. Armstrong and the other fellow in Chicago, Mitchell, used the Harry B.J. But I've never had my hands on one of them. Oh, that's fine. It's pretty good. So that's a Harry B.J., a silver-plated trombone. It has a small bell. Any number on the mouthpiece? Five. Number five? You know that, huh? You know what kind of a mouthpiece it is, huh? I think this is five. Oh, yeah. This is a... Hold the slide so I don't drop that. This is one of the real elaborately carved... What do you call that? Engraved. Engraved, yeah. How long have you had that? Columbia patented. Harry, H-A-R-R-Y, then capital B, period, J-A-Y. I didn't even know how that was spelled.
Harry B.J.
Company. Oh. Chicago. Harry B.J. Company, Chicago.
I traded a fellow by the name of Mike Riley for that trombone in 27. At the Elks Convention in Cleveland, Ohio.
That wouldn't be the Mike Riley that wrote Music Goes Round and Round. I don't know. What he did... The white fella?
No, this is a color...
No, he was a white fella. He used to play in New York.

And this fella played banjo and trombone. He had this one, and I had a handmade blessing made in Elkhart, Indiana. I paid $2.25 for the blessing, and he paid $2.25 for that one. And he had a weight, balance weight here.
Yes.

So he said to me, Henry, let's see your trombone. I said, all right. Pick it up, and he ran over a scale or two. He said, try mine. I tried this thing. I scratched my head. I said, gee, this thing has some tone to it. So he said, you want to use it today? I said, I don't care. We played from 9 o'clock till 6 in the evening on a parade. The Elks Parade in Cleveland, Ohio, in 26. So I came in. I threw the trombone on the bed, took the mouthpiece, put it in my pocket, walked out, changed chords, and was gone. Next morning, I saw him again. He said, how do you like my trombone? I said, it's fine. I said, how do you like mine? He said, man, that thing you got's jammed up. He said, how do you like to trade? I said, all right with me. I said, what you want? He said, let's trade instrument for instrument. He took my instrument and I took that. I don't think I had a bad job either.
No? It's nice. Still in good shape?
Oh, yeah, sure.
Plating all on it?
Well, I had it replated.
Oh, I see.
For the simple reason the plating was wearing off. And it cost me $50 to have it re-silver plated.
When you plated that, did they have to do anything to the engraving? No, no, they just replated it just like it was. The engraving stayed right on that way. How long ago was that you had it replaced?
I had it replated about seven, eight years. No?
Right here in town?
Yeah, on Crown Letts Street. You know where the music shop used to be across from... Oh, yes, I remember. Gus Myers on the... There's a bookstore there now.
Is it Philberto's or something like that? And what about all that green...
Well, this is a collar protector. See, to keep your collar... Instead of wearing a celluloid one, I found this ribbon in Crest.
Oh, is that in Crest?
They use it on the telephone wires. Oh, yeah. You know on telephone coils?
Yeah.

So I got it. Sonny Henry had a brown one, and I asked him where he got it, and I got it from here. Got a piece of that, and I put it on there. Well, you see the hand is here, and that keeps your hand from wearing a hole in here. Yeah. And your hand from wearing here, and then the platen don't get on your shirt collar, because when the platen gets on your shirt collar from the perspiration,

it makes a dark, dirty mark. It's about like they call that whalebone grip on violins. They make it out of whalebone or something. Is that curved or coiled around? It's wrapped around like it's plastic. You see it covered... It wasn't in one big straight piece or anything.
No, it's round like that.
It's already coiled up, yeah.
It's already coiled up. You see, you just wrap it around like that.
That's a rather small bell, isn't it, compared to some smaller...
Well, the only bell larger than this is a symphony model bass trombone. This is a tenor trombone.
Yeah. I thought Albert Warner's bell on that con, because it looked a little bigger, was it? Maybe just...
It's about the same size. There's no difference in the bell. It's a nice bell.
It's a nice bell.
No, you take a... They're making... The old people make a smaller bell. It's as large in here, but it's small here. See, they cut part of this rim off.
They almost have a smaller bell. They have a smaller bell than this. Never seen one. F.E.O.'s. Of course, it'd be a good trombone. Oh, yeah.
They're wonderful. But you take a trombone that has a big bore here, from here to here, you get more volume out of it for on the street.
In that last joint before the bell.
Yeah. Right in here. From there on up to the bell.
Up to the bell.
Of course, playing on the street is different to playing inside. For the simple reason you can fill up in this room with tone.
Yeah.

But when you get out on the street, you can't fill up the street out there. You have to put it out. Uh-huh. And then if the man don't use good, having good tongue action, because all notes is produced with the tongue and vibration of the lip with a light or heavy, with a light pressure of air, don't take them so much wind, but more tongue action than anything else.
What they call coupe de langue.
What was that? Coupe de langue in French.
What does that mean?
A stroke of the tongue. Oh, yeah.
And when you, the heavier stroke of the tongue, the louder the note.

The softer the stroke of the tongue, the softer the note. Some fellas never can control the wind action and the stroke of the tongue. That's what makes a good musician. When you can control the vibration of your lip and the stroke of your tongue. Because you can control. You got perfect control then. But if you got all heavy stroke, no control. Suppose you're playing a piano passage. You can't make it. You can't make piano with a double forty stroke. Or a triple forty stroke. You got three F's and you got three P's. You can't make the three P's and hitting three F's. And then you play, use one trombone for every five trumpets.
That's right, you don't have as many trombones.
One trombone can cover five trumpets. And you support to have five clarinets for every trumpet. Oh, yeah.
Yeah, and some of the big bands, the big concert bands, they do, yeah. Yeah.

So when you say music, you have something to contend with. Don't say you're just blowing the instrument. Now I was a Liberian for a band for seven years. Which band was that? The Elks Band in Chicago. Chicago. I can look at a man's instrument. You tell me what instrument you play, and I can get in, go into any stack of music and find the music you can play on that instrument, if you can play it. Now you take trombones, if you're short on trombone parts, you take oboe parts and give them to the trombone players. All you have to do is ignore the clef sign and play as written. If you have extra saxophone players, you take the treble clef trombone part and give it to the saxophone, the tenor saxophone players, and play it as written. It's already in the treble clef. You don't have to change nothing. Just read as written.

I was going to ask about the brass bands you've played with here. You're now a member of the Eureka Band, we know. Had you played much with some of the other brass bands down here a few years ago? I never met you until a couple years ago, I think.

I've played with George Williams. I've played with John Kazma several times. I've played with several mixed bands out of the union. Anything they have in town that they want to play. The business agent will tell you, well, who you got in the front there? Well, you got a chick up there, you don't need nobody else.
Any of them go, I can play with them. I wonder some of the dance bands that you've played with in New Orleans here, can you remember some of the musicians that you've played dances with?
I played with old Paul Beaulieu several times. We played a concert with Alphonse Picoult.
By the way, do you know where Beaulieu lives?
Beaulieu lives on, I think it's 1129 or 1128 North Robeson Street. North Robeson. Paul Beaulieu.
We must see him some of these days, I've never met him.

Yeah, he's a little slender brown-skinned fellow. He's a former postal employee, he's retired now. And you say you played with Picoult. Yeah, I played with Alphonse Picoult. We played a concert out at Xavier Prep, Xavier College out here. Oh, yeah. And I played a few dance jobs, but there don't be many of them no more. Mostly brass bands. Mostly brass bands. They had the dance work, well, it'll be all right. Look like the people don't go for it, they just go for those boxes. Yeah. Arthur Follett's.
Oh, to change the subject, do you have any favorite trombone of all the different people you've heard any place in the country? Who do you like?
Well, the trombone players I like. I like that fella Tommy Dorsey. I like that other fella Higginbottom. And I like that boy in Chicago. What we was talking about. Roy Palmer.
Roy Palmer. Yeah. I remember you mentioned to me.
Yeah, I like them fellas. And the fella would taught me he ought to play trombone. Old Charlie Clay, that man was great. He was great. He's passed on now.

You were mentioning to me one time about playing that pieces are all in the lower register, the trombone, like in the lower positions. Talk to me about that in our years. Can we say anything about that? Like in the sixth and seventh position?

Well, the notes made on the trombone in the second position can be made in the seventh position. Now you make F, C, F, C, A, F, and C down in the sixth position. But you can make the, if you read, if you don't want to make the C here, you can make it here. In the third position. Now you don't, in playing trombone, you play mostly from the fifth position to the closed position. For the simple reason you don't have, you can read the C that's made in the sixth position, but play it in the third position. You make C sharp in the fifth, you make C sharp in the second. Now if you're making B flat and C sharp, you make it right in the fifth position. Why change to come up here when you can make B flat and C sharp right here? B flat, C sharp, F sharp right there. You make G flat there. So you don't have to, you don't have to do no change.
You don't have to keep sliding all over the place.

You don't have to keep running all over the slide. There's no way you make the notes on the slide. You can't make B flat but one place, that's right here. You can make F here and you can make F here and you can make F here above the staff. That's the third space above the staff. But it's easier to make F here than it is to make it here or here.
Easier in the first position.

Because it's natural. That's a natural position for F. But it can be made there. But you have to be accurate on your slides. Now I just take these two fingers and move the slides. I don't need the, the slide is moved, see?
Yeah, it works nice and easy, you don't need much. Just with the fingers.

You see some fellas with their arms going like this, playing a trombone. It's all from here. All from the wrist. All from the wrist. This is when you eat, you eat from the wrist. You play from the wrist. When you iron, you iron from whatever you do. This part of the arm, the forearm is only used as a medium to move it where you want it.
Yeah. All you show the vibrania all comes from here. That's all the vibrania comes from here. That's all the vibrania comes from here.
That's all the vibrato comes from here.
Yeah, sounds nice.
Well, this instrument's got a nice tone. All you gotta do is keep it cleaned out.
How do you clean your trombone? What do you use to clean your trombone?
Well, I take this part, take a swab, run down here with some kerosene oil.
Through the bell and all, big swab?
Through the bell and big brush on the swab, and I'll go down in there. Then I clean.
Take the slide off.
You can look through these slides. Oh, that looks through the light.
Oh, yeah, sure, yes, I know how that is.
Look through to the light.
Yeah, it looks nice and clean in there.
See how they shine? Yeah. Take a, push that through there, and it takes all the inside out, all the stuff on the inside. Mm-hmm. Then I push it down and through here.
Down to the outside of the slide. Out to the casing.

Mm-hmm. Then after when I do that, I take and wrench it out with some lukewarm water and almond hammer brand cooking soda. Yeah, yeah, cooking soda. And that sweetens up the tone. That sweetens it up. Yeah. And after you pass that cooking soda through there and play, sure. Yeah, just like a brand new instrument. That's true.
Well, when you play with a dance band, I suppose you have sort of a different technique. Do you still play, if you play with a dance band now, do you still play a band style or what style?
I play whatever style the drum will be.
Oh, you go by the drums?
You go by the drum beat. Whatever. If you say one, two, three, four, one, two, three, four, you play that when it hit, you're on that bouncing style.
But if it's a slow, like a blues or something?
Well, you play according to the beat, tempo, or the drum. The drum and the bass. The bass is the foundation.
Would you say like you play a variation on the bass?
Well, not quite a variation on the bass, but you play an obligato to the bass.
Obligato.

Well, obligato to the trombone, to the trumpet. Of course, when you're playing music, it's just a conversation of instruments. Either one asks the question, and the other one answers it. If the basses ask it, the trumpets and the reeds answer it. If they ask it, you answer it. Sometimes the piano may ask the question, and some of the others answer it. But it all has to be done in harmony and in unison.
Well, as you're playing, you're listening to all the other instruments.

Oh, yeah. Well, when you're playing, if I'm playing too loud, in fact, if I'm playing so I can't hear the man sitting third to me, I'm playing too loud. And then another thing, you find thousands of musicians that are musically deaf. Seems like it sometimes. Now, I know a fellow by the the name of Harper that played with Louis Armstrong back in 26 or Armstrong back in 26 or 27, I don't remember which it was, but that man was musically deaf. And he had to always play under the other fella to keep from overplaying the man that was playing there. And he was a beautiful second trumpet player.
